findings.title: No tests exercise any of the cap-enforcement paths
findings.evidence: The only size enforcement in the loop is 'if total > max_bytes:' followed by the raise, and no test file accompanies this new module (no test commands were run).
findings.recommendation: Add tests covering: declared length above cap, streamed body above cap (server omitting/understating Content-Length), unparsable Content-Length falling through to the streaming check, body exactly equal to max_bytes (must succeed), empty body, and max_bytes < 1 raising ValueError. A fake response object or a local http.server endpoint is sufficient.

findings.title: Hardcoded UTF-8 decode rejects non-UTF-8 or truncated bodies with UnicodeDecodeError
findings.evidence: The return statement joins the raw bytes and decodes as UTF-8 unconditionally: 'return b"".join(chunks).decode("utf-8")' — the Content-Type charset (and requests' response.encoding) is ignored, and a body whose final bytes are cut mid-character raises UnicodeDecodeError instead of returning text or a clear domain error.
findings.recommendation: Derive the encoding from response.encoding/notes, or accept an encoding parameter defaulting to UTF-8, and document/handle decode failure (e.g. wrap UnicodeDecodeError in a dedicated exception) so callers are not surprised by a raw UnicodeDecodeError.

findings.title: Server-controlled Content-Length can spuriously reject a body that would fit
findings.evidence: The up-front check trusts the header absolutely: 'if int(declared) > max_bytes:' raises ResponseTooLarge before any bytes are read, so a misconfigured proxy or hostile server that overstates Content-Length makes fetch_text fail even when the actual payload is far below the cap — exactly the lie the streaming check already handles correctly.
findings.recommendation: Since the streamed total is authoritative, either drop the hard failure on the declared header (use it only as an early-abort heuristic when it is safe) or document explicitly that an overstated Content-Length causes rejection; at minimum cover this case in tests so the behaviour is intentional.

findings.title: timeout is per-read, not a total deadline, so a slow trickle holds the call
findings.evidence: 'with requests.get(url, timeout=timeout, stream=True) as response:' passes a single scalar timeout, which requests applies per connect/read interval; a server sending a few bytes every timeout-1 seconds keeps the loop alive for roughly max_bytes * timeout (about 115 days at default 1 MB / 10 s) without ever exceeding the size cap.
findings.evidence_quote: with requests.get(url, timeout=timeout, stream=True) as response:
findings.recommendation: Bound total wall-clock time: record a start time and abort the read loop when elapsed exceeds a deadline, or expose a separate total_timeout parameter and check it each iteration.

findings.title: No scheme/redirect restriction or redirect cap (SSRF surface if url is caller-supplied)
findings.evidence: requests.get with default settings follows up to 30 redirects: 'with requests.get(url, timeout=timeout, stream=True) as response:' — no allow_redirects control or allowlist is applied. This is only a concern when the URL comes from untrusted input, which the diff does not establish.
findings.evidence_quote: with requests.get(url, timeout=timeout, stream=True) as response:
findings.recommendation: Add a max_redirects/allow_redirects parameter (or document that callers must validate URLs) if this helper will be fed user- or tenant-supplied URLs.
